title: Destruction of Gaza Court System Strips Women of Their Rights
author: Rasha Abou jalal

GAZA CITY--Standing before the rubble of the Palace of Justice in central
Gaza, Salma Abdel Hadi was overwhelmed by a profound sense of helplessness.
Since her husband's killing last year, the 38-year-old mother of six has been
unable to secure inheritance rights for herself and her children to help
provide food and clothing in the midst of a genocide.

The Israeli military deliberately destroyed the Palace of Justice in Al-Zahra
City early in the war, rigging the court complex with explosives and
[demolishing](https://twitter.com/i/status/1731627015084679562) the entire
structure on December 4, 2023. Abdel Hadi's husband was killed in an Israeli
airstrike in August 2025, leaving her alone to raise and feed their children
in the Nuseirat refugee camp--and with no functioning court system, accessing
any of her late husband's money or property has been all but impossible.

"My children need their rights more than ever," Abdel Hadi told Drop Site
News, clasping her hands together in anguish. "But today I find myself facing
a question to which I have no answer: How can I protect my children's right to
inherit from their father if the place that is supposed to provide me with a
document proving that right has been reduced to rubble?"

In the three years of Israel's genocide in Gaza, the military has
systematically destroyed most of the enclave, including residential
neighborhoods, hospitals, schools and universities, bakeries, water systems,
electrical grids, along with most of Gaza's governmental, judicial, and
bureaucratic infrastructure. The lack of a functioning judicial system in Gaza
has particularly affected Palestinian women, who face a series of seemingly
insurmountable legal and bureaucratic obstacles to secure legal rights like
inheritance, divorce, alimony, property rights, and more.

Abdel Hadi said she is entitled to an inheritance of approximately $5,000 held
in her late husband's bank account, yet she cannot access the funds without an
inheritance certificate issued by the court. The delays in establishing
inheritance rights from her husband for herself and her children also allowed
members of his family to take control of some of his property. "My husband's
brother seized my husband's car without any legal right, and I was unable to
recover it through the judicial process because the courts are not
functioning," she said.

She estimates recovering ownership of the car and selling it could fetch as
much as $20,000. For a family that has lost its breadwinner and sole source of
income, the funds are critical and could make it possible to move out of the
tent where they are living and into a rented home, afford more food, and even
set aside whatever they can for the children's future.

Abdel Hadi also needs official documentation in order to obtain any assistance
or financial rights connected to their father, and prevent their property from
being disposed of without legal oversight. Aside from the car, the family owns
a 300-meter plot of land located near the Nuseirat camp where Abdel Hadi has
pitched a tent. In the absence of any documents, Abdel Hadi is unable as a
widow to safeguard her own social and economic rights or those of her
children.

"I want to get my children out of the tents and provide them with a home where
we can live, food to satisfy their hunger, and savings that will help them
continue their education when they reach university age," Abdel Hadi said.

In Gaza, the Sharia court is the authority that handles divorce, alimony,
custody, and guardianship cases, and issues documents establishing
inheritance, widowhood, death, and marriage. When these procedures are
suspended or become inaccessible, legal rights become pending claims that are
difficult to prove or enforce. Women in Gaza are bearing the brunt of Israel's
attack on the court system, particularly widows, divorced women, and women
caring for minors. The war has killed husbands and breadwinners, separated
families, and destroyed marriage documents and other files. In this vacuum,
women find themselves forced to negotiate with other parties and bargain over
their rights.

[A December 2025
report](https://pchrgaza.org/ar/%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B1%D9%83%D8%B2-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%81%D9%84%D8%B3%D8%B7%D9%8A%D9%86%D9%8A-%D9%84%D8%AD%D9%82%D9%88%D9%82-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A5%D9%86%D8%B3%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%8A%D8%B5%D8%AF%D8%B1-%D8%AA-5/)
by the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights found that "the suspension of
Sharia courts and the halt in receiving new cases as a result of the Israeli
attack have devastating effects on the situation of women in the Gaza Strip,
in the absence of any institutional alternatives capable of addressing
personal status cases. Women have become unable to pursue cases involving
separation, alimony or custody, leaving them in a legally suspended and
unstable situation."

The report noted that these circumstances have "exacerbated women's
psychological, social and economic suffering, made them more vulnerable to
marginalization and exploitation, and even pushed many of them to relinquish
their rights involuntarily as a result of the lack of avenues for legal
redress and the collapse of the formal protection system." It added, "women
have paid the highest price for the disruption of the judiciary, losing their
Sharia, economic and social rights and being subjected to continuous legal and
psychological injustice in the absence of institutional protection and
support."

In August 2023, two months before Israel's genocidal assault began, Aida
Hamid's husband left her. He offered to grant her a divorce in exchange for
her giving up her financial rights, including her deferred dowry, and other
rights she was legally entitled to.

"I refused to give up my Sharia rights in order to obtain the divorce so I
decided to file a lawsuit that would guarantee me a divorce while preserving
my legal rights," Hamid, 32, told Drop Site. "However, the outbreak of war,
the destruction of the courts and the disruption of judicial work left my case
unresolved and suspended."

Without any recourse in court, Hamid, who lives in Gaza City, has been left in
limbo. Not only has she been denied financial rights, such as a deferred dowry
and alimony, which she estimates at some 7,000 Jordanian dinars (about
$9,900), she has remained legally married, preventing her from finding a new
partner and marrying again.

"More than three years have passed without my case being resolved, leaving me
trapped in an unresolved social and legal situation," she said. "I have been
abandoned by my husband, and I do not have a court ruling ending the marriage,
which has turned my life into complete chaos."

Financial rights are more than just abstract legal entitlements for Hamid, but
instead are a vital resource that would help her secure basic needs and cost
of living as the genocide enters its fourth year.

"Receiving my deferred dowry and alimony would grant me a degree of financial
independence and reduce my dependence on others for my living expenses,
especially since I have been living in a state of legal and social limbo for
over three years due to the courts being closed," Halid said.

Mohammad Shehadeh, a lawyer who specializes in civil and Sharia cases, told
Drop Site that the effective incapacitation of the Sharia judiciary in Gaza
has "disrupted the lives of thousands of women and left them facing a legal
and social vacuum that threatens their rights and the rights of their
children."

Widows need a series of documents to establish their rights, such as proof of
the husband's death or filing a missing person claim, followed by obtaining an
inheritance certificate and proof of widowhood, and guardianship or legal
authority over any children.

"When the court is absent or the document is lost, the rights of women and
children are no longer protected by law, but instead become vulnerable to
family pressure, seizure or forced relinquishment," Shehadeh said. He added
that child custody cases are becoming increasingly complicated, particularly
when a husband is killed or goes missing, leading to disputes between the wife
and the husband's relatives over the care of the children and the management
of their inheritance. Abandoned women also face difficulties obtaining rulings
on separation and divorce, alimony, child custody or visitation rights.
Existing judgments are also difficult to enforce with no authority capable of
compelling payments or handing over documents.

There may also be unforeseen long term consequences of a nonfunctioning
judiciary that are not immediately apparent, Shehadeh warned. "A judicial file
that is lost today may turn tomorrow into a prolonged dispute over a home,
land, inheritance or custody, and proving the right may become more difficult
as time passes," he said, adding that some women may be compelled to accept
unfair settlements or relinquish their rights in exchange for a quick
resolution to a legal issue.

As with much else in Gaza, the damage to the Sharia judicial system in
Israel's assault has been devastating. Around half of all court premises have
been completely destroyed, according to Dr. Omar Nofal, the head of the Sharia
Court of Appeal in Gaza. Three of 30 judges have been killed along with 20
judicial staff members. A large part of the courts' paper archives, including
historical records and documents, has been burned or destroyed.

And as with nearly all Palestinians in Gaza, most judicial staff have been
displaced, forcing them to work from their places of shelter or temporary
locations, turning even simple bureaucratic procedures into an ordeal.

"We established three temporary locations in the Gaza Strip that operate as
courts, though their role is limited to receiving and registering lawsuits,"
Nofal said. "Because of the difficult circumstances resulting from the war,
judges have completed only a very small fraction of these cases, while most
cases have yet to be heard. Some of them have been registered for more than a
year without being considered."

Nofal also stressed that women face particular obstacles in cases involving
separation or divorce, spousal and child alimony, custody, guardianship, and
inheritance.

"When documents are lost or access to the court becomes impossible, the
children's money and the family's rights remain suspended, and the woman may
be forced to relinquish her rights," Nofal said. He also highlighted that even
if women obtain court rulings establishing their rights, they face major
obstacles in securing those rights in practice.

"Even if a woman obtains a court ruling establishing her right--for example,
if a divorced woman obtains her right to alimony or custody of her children--
there are no executive bodies to enforce the court order because the Israeli
army is pursuing the police authorities in Gaza," he said.

Police authorities in Gaza that are responsible for law enforcement have been
targeted by Israel in repeated attacks. Between January and August 2026, the
UN recorded at least 18 Israeli attacks against police personnel in Gaza,
resulting in the killing of at least 77 Palestinians, including 57 police
personnel, six children and four women. The attacks have targeted police
headquarters, posts, and vehicles, and appear to be escalating, with six of
them being carried out since June.

On August 19, an Israeli airstrike targeted a temporary municipal police
headquarters in Gaza City, killing eight police officers, including Fatena Al-
Sahhar, the head of the Women's Police in Gaza Governorate, as well as a
13-year-old girl.

"Under international humanitarian law, police personnel are civilians
protected against attacks. Targeting them is a war crime," the UN said in a
statement.

One year into the so-called "ceasefire," Israel continues to violate the
agreement on a daily basis, continuing its attacks on Palestinians and
preventing any reconstruction, including of Gaza's social, governmental, and
judicial institutions.

"With the absence of the judiciary, I have been left without a ruling to end
my marriage and without any means of claiming my rights," Abdel Hadi said. "I
feel as though my life has completely stopped along with the suspension of the
courts' work."
